To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the detection of minihalo dark matter annihilation is very challenging, but not out of the reach of GLAST.
the gamma-ray signal from dark matter annihilating in minihalos in the Milky Way will be very weak and difficult to detect, even for the most optimistic scenarios.
the detection of gamma rays from dark-matter annihilation within minihalos in the Milky Way is extremely challenging for the GLAST satellite, even if the neutralino mass is as low as 50 GeV.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the annihilation of dark matter particles in the minihalos that constitute the Galactic substructure.
the study of the gamma rays from dark-matter annihilation in the minihalos.
the study of gamma rays from the annihilation of neutralinos in the Galactic halo and the search of minihaloes in the sky.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the detection of minihalo gamma-ray emission is not feasible in the near future.
, while the possibility of a detection is still open, the chances are slim.
the gamma-ray flux from minihalos cannot be detected by GLAST, but that it can be detected by a next-generation gamma-ray telescope with an order of magnitude better sensitivity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the minihalos are very difficult to be detected in gamma-rays from the dark matter annihilation, but they can provide an important constraint on dark matter properties, especially for the annihilation channel of b-bar b, which is the best candidate for a detection of the minihaloes.

, if minihalos exist, the GLAST sensitivity is not enough to detect them, unless the annihilation cross-section of dark matter is much larger than the thermal relic cross-section, which is the standard value for the neutralinos in the supersymmetric models.
, if the minihalos are not detectable by gamma-ray telescopes, then they are not the main source of gamma-ray emission from dark matter annihila- tion in our Galaxy.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the gamma-ray flux from dark matter annihiliation within minihalos can be detected only if the annihilation cross section is larger than the thermal one, i.e. if the minihalos are populated by non-thermal dark matter particles.
the detection of gamma-ray emission from dark matter annihlation occurring within minihalos requires a much better angular resolution than that of GLAST.

, even in the most optimistic scenario, GLAST will be able to detect only the most massive minihalos in the innermost part of the Galaxy, while the bulk of the minihalos will be beyond the reach of the experiment.
